sessions.title: Vectors are typed coordinate objects
sessions.focus: Introduce real coordinate vectors and type-safe arithmetic without using matrices.
sessions.purpose: Introduce real coordinate vectors and type-safe arithmetic without using matrices.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret coordinate operations while checking ambient dimension and the zero-vector type.
sessions.principalObstacle: A tuple of numbers is treated as an untyped bag; a scalar zero or wrong-length tuple is silently accepted.
requiredOwnership: Compute scalar multiples and sums of equal-dimension real coordinate vectors.
Reject an addition between vectors of different ambient dimensions.
Identify the zero vector of a specified ambient dimension rather than a scalar zero.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes a same-space arithmetic task into an embedding/equality audit between two coordinate spaces.
inScope: Introduce real coordinate vectors and type-safe arithmetic without using matrices.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute and interpret coordinate operations while checking ambient dimension and the zero-vector type.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A list of components can record a multicomponent change, but its length and coordinate order are part of its type. In R^n a vector is an ordered n-tuple of real numbers. Equality requires the same n and each corresponding component equal. A scalar is one real number; the zero vector 0_n=(0,...,0) has n components.

Define. For u=(u1,...,un), v=(v1,...,vn) in the same R^n, set u+v=(u1+v1,...,un+vn) and cu=(cu1,...,cun) for real c. Addition and subtraction require the same n; multiplication by a scalar retains n. A two-component vector cannot be added to a three-component vector by silently padding a zero.

Worked example. Let u=(2,-1,3), v=(-1,4,0) in R^3. Then 2u-v=(4,-2,6)-(-1,4,0)=(5,-6,6). The zero vector here is (0,0,0), so u+(-u)=0_3; the scalar 0 merely supplies the multiplier in 0u=0_3. All three displayed vectors still have three components.

Guided practice. For p=(1,3), q=(-2,5), compute p+2q: 2q=(-4,10), hence p+2q=(-3,13) in R^2. A proposed sum p+(0,0,1) is undefined: lengths two and three differ.

Distinction check. Arithmetic on matching lengths is well-typed, but an application may impose further unit or coordinate-meaning constraints; those enter next.

sessions.title: Points, displacements and component meaning
sessions.focus: Relate coordinates to geometry and to non-geometric component tables while keeping operations meaningful.
sessions.purpose: Relate coordinates to geometry and to non-geometric component tables while keeping operations meaningful.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct displacements and use componentwise changes while distinguishing points from free vectors.
sessions.principalObstacle: Adding two positions as though their sum were another position, or mixing quantities with mismatched component meanings.
requiredOwnership: Compute a displacement from two coordinate points in a declared order.
Recover an endpoint by adding a displacement to a point.
Reject a numerically possible but semantically mismatched componentwise operation.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from spatial displacement to a data schema with same-length but semantically mismatched coordinate order.
inScope: Relate coordinates to geometry and to non-geometric component tables while keeping operations meaningful.
sessions.exitCondition: Construct displacements and use componentwise changes while distinguishing points from free vectors.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Coordinates can label a location P, while a vector can describe a change. These may share notation but play different roles. Once an origin and axes are chosen, the displacement from P to Q is Q-P; adding that displacement to P reaches Q. Reversing the order reverses the direction. This is a local convention, not a claim that every data vector is a physical arrow.

Define. A typed component table records coordinate name and unit, such as (temperature change in °C, pressure change in kPa). Compatible changes may be added componentwise; a vector with different meanings in the same positions is not a meaningful sum until an explicit conversion/relabeling is supplied. Numeric dimensions alone are necessary but not sufficient for semantic compatibility.

Worked example. In a plane with coordinates measured in metres, P=(1,-2) and Q=(4,3) give displacement d=Q-P=(3,5). Starting at Q and applying -d=(-3,-5) returns Q-d=(1,-2)=P. A vector (3,5) could alternatively encode two unrelated measurements; the arithmetic representation alone does not fix its interpretation.

Guided practice. If A=(-2,1) and B=(0,4), then B-A=(2,3), and A+(2,3)=B. The reverse displacement A-B=(-2,-3) starts at B.

Distinction check. Two location labels need not be added as if the sum were a location with a physical meaning; displacement plus location has the intended endpoint meaning here. Stating coordinate order and units is part of an application answer.

sessions.title: Linear combinations are parameterized families
sessions.focus: Move from a fixed vector calculation to coefficients that generate a family of vectors.
sessions.purpose: Move from a fixed vector calculation to coefficients that generate a family of vectors.
sessions.centralCapability: Form and expand a general linear combination and distinguish arbitrary real coefficients from one selected example.
sessions.principalObstacle: Calling one computed sum the entire family, or silently restricting coefficients without the problem stating it.
requiredOwnership: Expand a two-generator linear combination as a function of arbitrary real coefficients.
Produce a member of that family for specified coefficients.
Distinguish the full unrestricted family from a restricted-coefficient subset.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer adds a coefficient constraint and requires separating a restricted family from the unrestricted generated set.
inScope: Move from a fixed vector calculation to coefficients that generate a family of vectors.
sessions.exitCondition: Form and expand a general linear combination and distinguish arbitrary real coefficients from one selected example.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Once vectors can be scaled and added, ask what changes when the scalars vary. For u and v in the same R^n, au+bv is a linear combination; unless a restriction is stated, a and b range independently over all real numbers. One chosen pair (a,b) gives one vector, while the expression with variables describes many.

Worked example. For u=(1,2,-1) and v=(0,1,3), au+bv=(a,2a+b,-a+3b). At a=2,b=-1 this is (2,3,-5). The zero choice a=b=0 yields (0,0,0). Restricting to a+b=1 would give a different family, not the unrestricted set. Coefficient choices need not be unique if the generators later prove redundant.

Connect. In a plane, multiples of one nonzero vector trace a line through the origin. Two vectors pointing in genuinely different directions can generate a plane. The coordinate expression, rather than a drawing alone, settles which targets are actually reachable. That exact question is next.

Guided practice. For p=(2,0) and q=(1,1), cp+dq=(2c+d,d). At c=-1,d=3 this becomes (1,3); at c=d=0 it is (0,0). Allowing negative coefficients is part of unrestricted linear combinations.

Distinction check. A constraint such as c,d≥0 or c+d=1 defines a subset of the possible combinations; it is not silently present in the definition of span.

sessions.title: Span membership needs a coefficient witness
sessions.focus: Define the span as a set and turn a target-membership claim into a coefficient existence claim.
sessions.purpose: Define the span as a set and turn a target-membership claim into a coefficient existence claim.
sessions.centralCapability: Decide elementary span membership by matching coordinates and producing a witness when one exists.
sessions.principalObstacle: A target is declared reachable by appearance, or one successful target is confused with spanning the whole ambient space.
requiredOwnership: Represent span{u,v} as a family with arbitrary real coefficient choices.
For a specified target in an elementary span, solve coordinate constraints and give explicit coefficient witnesses.
Explain why witnessing one target in a span does not establish that the generators span the entire ambient space.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from a single target to a universally parameterized family and requires a symbolic witness for every member.
inScope: Define the span as a set and turn a target-membership claim into a coefficient existence claim.
sessions.exitCondition: Decide elementary span membership by matching coordinates and producing a witness when one exists.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A library of generators answers a reachability question: which targets can be assembled by scaling and adding its vectors? The span of u and v is the set {au+bv : a,b∈R}. It contains infinitely many vectors in most nonzero cases, including zero; it is neither the two-item list {u,v} nor any one sample sum.

Translate. To prove that a target t is in a span, exhibit real coefficients that make au+bv=t. This is an existential statement, so one verified witness suffices. Coordinate comparison turns it into simultaneous scalar equations. A picture of a line or plane may suggest the answer, but the equations supply an exact check. Showing one target is reachable does not show every vector in the surrounding R^n is reachable.

Worked example. For u=(1,0,3) and v=(0,1,-2), a general combination is (a,b,3a-2b), the plane of triples whose third coordinate equals three times the first minus twice the second. The target t=(3,-2,13) has a=3,b=-2, and 3(3)-2(-2)=13, so t=3u-2v. This is one membership certificate; it does not claim the two vectors generate every triple in R^3.

Guided practice. Let p=(1,1) and q=(1,-1). To make (4,2), solve c+d=4 and c-d=2: adding gives c=3, then d=1. Check 3p+q=(4,2). The coefficient witness is more informative than “looks like it is in the plane.”

Distinction check. Membership of one specified target is ∃ coefficients for that target. Spanning all of R^n requires ∀ targets ∃ coefficients; the quantifiers cannot be swapped or inferred from a single success.

sessions.title: Nonmembership and changing generators
sessions.focus: Prove a target unreachable by an invariant or inconsistent coefficient equations, then test how generators change reachability.
sessions.purpose: Prove a target unreachable by an invariant or inconsistent coefficient equations, then test how generators change reachability.
sessions.centralCapability: Give a valid obstruction to span membership and distinguish redundant from enlarging generators.
sessions.principalObstacle: Failure to find coefficients is reported as proof none exist, or one extra generator is assumed to enlarge the span.
requiredOwnership: Derive a necessary coordinate condition for a generated set and use its failure to prove nonmembership.
Demonstrate by a witness or obstruction whether an added generator changes what is reachable.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer reverses nonmembership by adding a new direction and asks for a strict-enlargement witness.
inScope: Prove a target unreachable by an invariant or inconsistent coefficient equations, then test how generators change reachability.
sessions.exitCondition: Give a valid obstruction to span membership and distinguish redundant from enlarging generators.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A membership witness is existential, but nonmembership demands exclusion of every possible coefficient choice. One reliable route is an invariant: derive an equation every generated vector must obey, then display the target violating it. “I could not solve it” is not an argument.

Worked example. Let u=(1,1,0), v=(0,1,1). Any au+bv=(a,a+b,b) satisfies middle = first + third. Thus (2,5,1) is outside the span because 5≠2+1, regardless of a,b. Adding w=(1,2,1)=u+v does not enlarge the set: every c w contributes c u+c v, and old combinations remain available by choosing c=0. Adding z=(0,1,0), by contrast, reaches the former missing target: 2u+v+2z=(2,5,1). This proves a concrete enlargement, without claiming an algorithm for arbitrary inputs.

Guided practice. For p=(1,0,1), q=(0,1,1), all combinations satisfy third = first + second. Therefore (1,1,3) is impossible. The proposed new generator p+q is already reachable, so including it leaves the span unchanged.

Distinction check. To show the new span is strictly larger it suffices to exhibit one new reachable vector known to be outside the old span. A redundant generator may increase the list length while adding no direction.

sessions.title: Subspaces require closure
sessions.focus: Use zero, addition and scalar closure to distinguish linear subspaces from translated or constrained sets.
sessions.purpose: Use zero, addition and scalar closure to distinguish linear subspaces from translated or constrained sets.
sessions.centralCapability: Verify an elementary real-coordinate set is a subspace or give a decisive closure counterexample.
sessions.principalObstacle: A line or plane is called a subspace based on appearance despite excluding zero or failing negative scaling.
requiredOwnership: Prove an elementary subset is a subspace by checking zero, addition and arbitrary real scalar closure.
Construct a valid counterexample showing a translated set is not a linear subspace.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes the homogeneous set into a translated affine set and asks for a counterexample and proof diagnosis.
inScope: Use zero, addition and scalar closure to distinguish linear subspaces from translated or constrained sets.
sessions.exitCondition: Verify an elementary real-coordinate set is a subspace or give a decisive closure counterexample.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A subspace H of R^n inherits vector addition and real scalar multiplication. Its zero vector must belong, and for any u,v in H and any real c, both u+v and cu must remain in H. Checking one pair is not a proof of closure; one legal failure is enough to refute it.

Worked example. H={(x,y,z)∈R^3:z=x-y}. Zero satisfies 0=0-0. If u=(x1,y1,x1-y1) and v=(x2,y2,x2-y2), their sum has third coordinate (x1+x2)-(y1+y2); cu has third coordinate cx1-cy1. Both remain in H for arbitrary inputs and real c. Moreover (x,y,x-y)=x(1,0,1)+y(0,1,-1), so the geometric plane and all-coefficient description agree.

Guided practice. K={(x,y)∈R²:x+y=1} contains (1,0) but not zero. Scaling (1,0) by 0 leaves K, so K is not a linear subspace. A translated line can be geometrically straight without being closed under vector operations.

Distinction check. A set given by a homogeneous linear coordinate condition can be a subspace when closure is proved; a similar-looking equation with a nonzero constant is not. M13 does not need nullspaces or matrix notation for this test.

sessions.title: Independence tests all zero combinations
sessions.focus: Introduce linear independence as a universal condition on coefficients and dependence as a nontrivial zero witness.
sessions.purpose: Introduce linear independence as a universal condition on coefficients and dependence as a nontrivial zero witness.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove or refute independence by solving the zero-combination equations, including exceptional parameter values.
sessions.principalObstacle: Checking only that each vector is nonzero or that one chosen combination is nonzero.
requiredOwnership: Prove independence by forcing every coefficient in a zero combination to vanish.
Identify and certify the parameter values where a vector pair becomes dependent.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes a fixed list into a parameter family requiring an exceptional-value classification.
inScope: Introduce linear independence as a universal condition on coefficients and dependence as a nontrivial zero witness.
sessions.exitCondition: Prove or refute independence by solving the zero-combination equations, including exceptional parameter values.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Every vector list produces zero by taking all coefficients zero. Independence asks whether this is the **only** way: for v1,...,vk, if c1v1+...+ckvk=0 then all ci=0. Dependence is the negation: produce at least one coefficient tuple not all zero whose combination is zero. “Each vector is nonzero” alone is insufficient.

Worked example. Let p=(1,0), q=(2,1). If ap+bq=(a+2b,b)=(0,0), the second coordinate forces b=0 and then the first forces a=0. Thus the pair is independent. If q were (2,0), the relation 2p-q=0 would witness dependence; checking the trivial relation alone would prove nothing.

Guided practice. For r=(1,2), s=(2,4), the coefficients (2,-1) give 2r-s=(0,0), so the pair is dependent. Neither the size of coefficients nor the order of vectors matters, only that the relation is genuinely nontrivial.

Distinction check. The claim “all coefficients zero works” is true for every list. Independence is an implication over *every* coefficient choice; dependence needs one explicit nontrivial witness.

sessions.title: Redundancy is collective
sessions.focus: Connect nontrivial zero relations with removable generators and expose the pairwise-inspection fallacy.
sessions.purpose: Connect nontrivial zero relations with removable generators and expose the pairwise-inspection fallacy.
sessions.centralCapability: Use a dependence certificate to identify a redundant member and prove span is preserved when it is removed.
sessions.principalObstacle: No two vectors are multiples, so the whole list is wrongly called independent.
requiredOwnership: Construct a three-vector dependence certificate even though no pair is parallel.
Prove a generator can be removed without changing the span by expressing it through the remaining vectors.
Derive a removable-generator statement from a nontrivial zero relation with a nonzero coefficient.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from explicit coordinates to an abstract supplied relation and asks what follows and what does not.
inScope: Connect nontrivial zero relations with removable generators and expose the pairwise-inspection fallacy.
sessions.exitCondition: Use a dependence certificate to identify a redundant member and prove span is preserved when it is removed.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Dependence is about a whole list. Three vectors can be dependent even if every pair is nonparallel. A nontrivial relation c1v1+...+ckvk=0 has some cj≠0, so vj=-(1/cj) times the sum of the other terms. This division is legal because that chosen coefficient is nonzero. Conversely, if vj is a combination of the others, moving all terms to one side produces a nontrivial relation with coefficient 1 on vj.

Worked example. Take p=(1,0,0), q=(0,1,0), r=(1,1,0). No pair is scalar multiples, but p+q-r=0. Because r=p+q, any ap+bq+cr=(a+c)p+(b+c)q. Thus dropping r preserves every reachable vector; the shorter list also remains inside the old span by taking c=0. Both inclusions, not just a picture, establish equality of spans.

Guided practice. Let u=(1,1), v=(2,0), w=(3,1). Since u+v-w=0, w can be removed. A combination 4u-v+2w becomes 6u+v after replacing w by u+v; check both coordinate results equal (8,6).

Distinction check. Pairwise nonparallel is necessary for independence of a nonzero pair, but it does not settle a list of three or more. A dependence relation has to be collective and nontrivial.

sessions.title: A basis spans and is independent
sessions.focus: Unify reachability and nonredundancy, then prove uniqueness of basis coordinates.
sessions.purpose: Unify reachability and nonredundancy, then prove uniqueness of basis coordinates.
sessions.centralCapability: Verify both basis conditions and derive unique coefficient representation.
sessions.principalObstacle: A spanning but redundant list or an independent but incomplete list is called a basis.
requiredOwnership: Verify a proposed basis by proving both independence and spanning of its named space.
Prove uniqueness of coordinates relative to an independent spanning list.
Diagnose which basis condition fails for an independent but incomplete list.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from basis construction to diagnosis of an incomplete list and a tempting redundant repair.
inScope: Unify reachability and nonredundancy, then prove uniqueness of basis coordinates.
sessions.exitCondition: Verify both basis conditions and derive unique coefficient representation.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A basis for a real vector space V is a list of vectors in V that is both independent and spans V. Spanning guarantees that each target has *some* representation; independence guarantees *at most one*. Both directions are needed. The basis list itself need not be unique.

Worked example. In R², e=(1,0) and f=(1,1) span because (x,y)=(x-y)e+yf for arbitrary real x,y. They are independent: ae+bf=(a+b,b)=0 forces b=0 then a=0. Thus they form a basis. If (x,y)=ae+bf=ce+df, subtracting gives (a-c)e+(b-d)f=0; independence forces a=c,b=d. This argument proves coordinate uniqueness for any independent list, not just this pair.

Guided practice. In R², (1,0),(0,1),(1,1) span but are dependent because the third is the sum of the first two. The singleton (1,0) is independent but does not span (0,1). Neither list is a basis of R².

Distinction check. A basis must have enough directions and no redundant directions. Coordinate numbers change with the chosen basis even when the underlying vector stays the same.

sessions.title: Construct bases and compare coordinates
sessions.focus: Build a basis of an elementary subspace from its parameterization and compute coordinates within that basis.
sessions.purpose: Build a basis of an elementary subspace from its parameterization and compute coordinates within that basis.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct a nonstandard basis and represent an element by unique relative coordinates.
sessions.principalObstacle: Ambient tuple entries are mistaken for coordinates in a chosen basis, or a generator is removed without a span proof.
requiredOwnership: Construct and verify a basis of a described elementary subspace of R³.
Compute a vector’s coordinates relative to that basis and distinguish them from its ambient triple.
Remove a redundant generator and still justify a basis and target coordinates.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from a defining equation with free basis construction to a redundant supplied library with several valid basis choices.
inScope: Build a basis of an elementary subspace from its parameterization and compute coordinates within that basis.
sessions.exitCondition: Construct a nonstandard basis and represent an element by unique relative coordinates.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A vector can lie in R³ while belonging to a two-parameter plane. To choose a basis, parameterize *every* vector in that plane and read off the coefficient directions. Then verify the directions are independent. The ambient triple represents the vector in the standard coordinates of R³; the shorter tuple [t]_B lists its coefficients in the chosen subspace basis.

Worked example. For H={(x,y,z):z=2x+y}, write (x,y,2x+y)=x(1,0,2)+y(0,1,1). These two directions span H. If a(1,0,2)+b(0,1,1)=0, the first two coordinates force a=b=0, proving independence. Thus B=((1,0,2),(0,1,1)) is a basis. The vector (1,2,4) has B-coordinates (1,2), not the ambient triple (1,2,4).

Guided practice. For K={(x,y,z):z=y}, every member is x(1,0,0)+y(0,1,1). The vectors are independent because their first two coordinates isolate the coefficients. In K, (3,-1,-1) has coordinates (3,-1) in this basis.

Distinction check. A different valid basis changes the coordinate tuple without changing the vector. Systematic change-of-basis matrices wait for M14; here direct coefficient solving is enough.

sessions.title: Dimension is invariant under basis choice
sessions.focus: Prove the finite replacement bound without matrices before using basis size as a space invariant.
sessions.purpose: Prove the finite replacement bound without matrices before using basis size as a space invariant.
sessions.centralCapability: Justify that finite bases of one real vector space have the same length, using a bounded replacement argument.
sessions.principalObstacle: A basis count is declared intrinsic from pictures or from an unowned rank theorem.
requiredOwnership: Explain why an independent list cannot be longer than a finite spanning list, using a valid replacement step.
Deduce equal length of any two finite bases of the same space by applying the bound both ways.
Use the bound to reject an impossible independent-list cardinality claim.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes to evaluating an unseen cardinality claim and the one-way meaning of a spanning-list size.
inScope: Prove the finite replacement bound without matrices before using basis size as a space invariant.
sessions.exitCondition: Justify that finite bases of one real vector space have the same length, using a bounded replacement argument.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. “Dimension is the number of vectors in a basis” needs a theorem: two bases could a priori have different sizes. We prove a finite replacement bound without elimination. Suppose B=(v1,...,vm) spans V and W=(w1,...,wn) is independent. After replacing k-1 members of B, maintain a spanning list containing w1,...,w(k-1) plus m-k+1 old members. Express wk using this spanning list. Some coefficient of an *old* member must be nonzero; otherwise wk is a combination of previous w’s, contradicting independence. Solve that expression for the old member and replace it by wk: every old generator is still reachable, so the new list spans. Repeat. We cannot replace more than m old members, so n≤m.

Worked example. In R² start from B=(e1,e2), and independent w1=(1,1), w2=(1,-1). Because w1=e1+e2, replace e1 and recover e1=w1-e2. In the new spanning list (w1,e2), w2=w1-2e2; the coefficient -2 is nonzero, so replace e2 and recover e2=(w1-w2)/2. The resulting two-vector list spans. This small example illustrates the general replacement, not a matrix algorithm.

Conclude. If B and C are both finite bases of V, C is independent and B spans, hence |C|≤|B|. Swap roles to get |B|≤|C|, so their sizes agree. That common size is dim(V).

Guided practice. If a space has a spanning list of two vectors, a proposed independent list of three is impossible by n≤m. This does not assert that every two-vector list is a basis: each condition still needs proof.

Distinction check. The theorem compares lists in the *same space*. A subspace of R³ can have a two-vector basis; ambient coordinate length three does not set its intrinsic dimension.

sessions.title: Subspace dimension and the zero case
sessions.focus: Apply invariant dimension to a plane inside R³ and to the zero space without conflating ambient length.
sessions.purpose: Apply invariant dimension to a plane inside R³ and to the zero space without conflating ambient length.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive finite subspace dimension from a proved basis and handle dimension zero correctly.
sessions.principalObstacle: A vector in R³ is declared three-dimensional regardless of its subspace or the zero vector is included in a basis.
requiredOwnership: Construct a basis for a specified plane in R³ and infer its dimension from the verified basis.
Distinguish a subspace’s intrinsic dimension from the coordinate length of its members.
Identify the empty list as a basis of the zero subspace and reject a zero-vector basis.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.
sessions.transferScope: Transfer changes from a nonzero plane to the exceptional zero subspace and the empty-basis convention.
inScope: Apply invariant dimension to a plane inside R³ and to the zero space without conflating ambient length.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive finite subspace dimension from a proved basis and handle dimension zero correctly.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Once all basis sizes agree, dimension counts independent directions of the space, not the number of coordinates used by an ambient representation. To assign a dimension, actually give a basis and verify span and independence. In the zero space {0}, the empty list has no nontrivial zero relation and its empty combination gives zero; by convention it is a basis of size zero. A list containing 0 is dependent, since 1·0=0.

Worked example. H={(x,y,z)∈R³:z=x-2y}. Every vector is x(1,0,1)+y(0,1,-2). These two directions are independent because their first two coordinates force any zero-combination coefficients to vanish. Thus dim(H)=2 even though each H-vector has three ambient entries. The full R³ has standard basis e1,e2,e3 and dimension 3.

Guided practice. For L={(x,y,z):x=0,y=0}, every vector is z(0,0,1). The nonzero generator (0,0,1) is independent, so dim(L)=1. If z must also equal zero, the resulting {0} has dimension zero and empty basis.

Distinction check. A line, a plane and all R³ can all contain three-component vectors while having dimensions 1, 2 and 3. The zero vector is in each but cannot appear in any independent basis.

sessions.title: The dot product and Euclidean length
sessions.focus: Define an algebraic scalar product of real coordinate vectors and derive length from positivity.
sessions.purpose: Define an algebraic scalar product of real coordinate vectors and derive length from positivity.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute dot products and norms with correct object types and dimension conditions.

requiredOwnership: Compute the Euclidean dot product of equal-dimension real vectors as a scalar.
Compute Euclidean norm from the self-dot product and handle the zero-vector case.
Reject a componentwise-vector answer masquerading as a dot product.

inScope: Define an algebraic scalar product of real coordinate vectors and derive length from positivity.

sessions.lesson:
Orient. Vector addition outputs a vector. The Euclidean dot product takes u,v in the same R^n and outputs a **scalar**: u·v=Σ(i=1 to n) ui vi. It is symmetric and linear in each argument because real-number multiplication and finite addition are; these are properties of the definition, not extra conventions.

Worked example. For u=(1,2,-2) and v=(2,0,1), u·v=1·2+2·0+(-2)·1=0, a scalar. The self-dot u·u=1+4+4=9, so ||u||=sqrt(u·u)=3. Also v·v=4+0+1=5 and ||v||=sqrt(5). Since Σui²≥0, norm is nonnegative and ||u||=0 exactly for u=0. A dot product of a two-vector with a three-vector is not defined under this rule.

Connect. Coordinatewise multiplication would give a vector (2,0,-2) here, not the dot product. To check distributivity, u·(v+w)=Σui(vi+wi)=Σui vi+Σui wi. This algebra matters before assigning any geometric interpretation.

Guided practice. For p=(2,-1), q=(-1,3), p·q=-2-3=-5; p·p=5 and ||p||=sqrt(5). The dot is a scalar even when it is negative; the norm is never negative.

Distinction check. A zero dot product between nonzero vectors will later encode perpendicularity; zero self-dot means the vector itself is zero. Neither fact makes the dot product a componentwise vector.

sessions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle bounds
sessions.focus: Prove the two Euclidean inequalities from positivity before treating normalized dot products as cosines.
sessions.purpose: Prove the two Euclidean inequalities from positivity before treating normalized dot products as cosines.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive and apply Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality with zero cases and hypotheses visible.
sessions.principalObstacle: Angle language is used to justify the bound that is needed to make the angle formula legitimate in higher dimensions.
entryPrerequisites: M01 nonnegative squares and scalar algebra
requiredOwnership: Prove |u·v|≤||u||||v|| for real equal-dimension vectors, including v=0.
Deduce ||u+v||≤||u||+||v|| from dot-product expansion and Cauchy–Schwarz.
Reject an impossible proposed dot product using the norm bound.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite real coordinate vectors with explicitly stated dimensions and coefficient conventions.

inScope: Prove the two Euclidean inequalities from positivity before treating normalized dot products as cosines.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive and apply Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality with zero cases and hypotheses visible.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. The normalized ratio (u·v)/(||u||||v||) should lie between -1 and 1 for nonzero vectors. Prove that fact algebraically before calling it a cosine. For v=0 the bound |u·v|≤||u||||v|| is 0≤0. For v≠0 let t=(u·v)/(v·v), a real scalar. Nonnegativity gives 0≤||u-tv||²=||u||²-2t(u·v)+t²||v||²=||u||²-(u·v)²/||v||². Multiply by positive ||v||² and take nonnegative square roots: |u·v|≤||u||||v||. This is a proof device with one scalar t, not an M15 projection algorithm.

Worked example. For u=(2,1), v=(1,-2), u·v=0, ||u||=||v||=sqrt(5); the inequality gives 0≤5. For a nontrivial case p=(2,0), q=(1,1), |p·q|=2≤2sqrt(2)=||p||||q||. The point is the all-vector proof above, not numerical checking.

Derive. Expand ||u+v||²=||u||²+2u·v+||v||²≤(||u||+||v||)². Both norms are nonnegative, so taking square roots yields ||u+v||≤||u||+||v||. Equality questions are optional here and must not be guessed from one picture.

Guided practice. If ||a||=3 and ||b||=4, |a·b|≤12; a report of a·b=13 is impossible. Also ||a+b||≤7. These statements do not reveal the actual dot product or norm of the sum.

Distinction check. A universal inequality is proved from the Euclidean dot product and its positivity; a few examples are checks, not the proof.

sessions.lesson:
Orient. Dot product was defined algebraically in S13. For nonzero planar vectors, the ordinary Euclidean law of cosines applied to the triangle with sides u,v,u-v says ||u-v||²=||u||²+||v||²-2||u||||v||cos θ, where θ is the angle between their directions. Algebraic expansion gives the same left side as ||u||²+||v||²-2u·v. Comparing yields cos θ=(u·v)/(||u||||v||). In R^n the ratio defines the Euclidean angle via arccos; S14 ensures it lies in [-1,1].

Worked example. For u=(2,0), v=(1,1), u·v=2, ||u||=2, ||v||=sqrt(2), so cos θ=1/sqrt(2) and θ=π/4. Scaling v by 5 changes the raw dot product from 2 to 10 but leaves the angle the same because its norm also scales by 5.

Guided practice. For a=(1,0), b=(-1,0), cos θ=-1 and θ=π. For a=(1,0), c=(0,1), cos θ=0 and θ=π/2. The direction comparison uses nonzero vectors.

Distinction check. If one vector is zero, its norm is zero and the displayed quotient is undefined. Although 0·v=0, a zero vector has no direction; do not assign a right angle to it. Angle is an interpretation under conditions, not the dot product’s definition.

sessions.focus: Use zero dot products to test orthogonality and compare raw versus normalized alignment.
sessions.purpose: Use zero dot products to test orthogonality and compare raw versus normalized alignment.

sessions.lesson:
Orient. In Euclidean R^n two vectors are algebraically orthogonal when their dot product is zero. If both are nonzero, S15 then gives cos θ=0 and a right angle. The zero vector is algebraically orthogonal to every vector under the zero-dot definition, but has no angle. This distinction prevents a definition from silently importing a geometric interpretation outside its domain.

Worked example. Compare u=(1,1) with v=(50,0) and w=(2,2). Raw dots are 50 and 4, respectively; nevertheless cos(u,v)=1/sqrt(2) and cos(u,w)=1. The smaller raw dot corresponds to stronger directional alignment because v has much larger magnitude. A nonzero vector z=(-1,1) has u·z=0 and is perpendicular to u.

Guided practice. For a=(1,2), b=(2,-1), a·b=2-2=0, and both are nonzero, so their angle is π/2. Replacing b by zero preserves the algebraic zero dot but removes the angle claim.

Distinction check. “Orthogonal” in this module means zero Euclidean dot product, not statistical independence. A directional similarity question uses a normalized ratio when vectors are nonzero; a magnitude question uses a norm or a context-specific scale.

sessions.lesson:
Orient. A synthesis task is not a list of memorized names. First ask what each vector represents and which generator directions are redundant. Separate the existential target-witness question from the universal basis question. Then decide whether a magnitude, dot product, normalized angle or zero-dot relation answers the geometric part. These decisions are available from earlier sessions; no matrix or projection algorithm is needed.

Worked example. Let p=(1,0,0), q=(0,1,1), r=(1,1,1)=p+q. The pair (p,q) is independent because first and second coordinates isolate coefficients; it spans the same library as all three because r is redundant. The target (2,-1,-1)=2p-q has relative coordinates (2,-1). Against d=(0,1,0), its dot is -1 and its cosine is -1/sqrt(6), since both norms are nonzero. This example shows the order of justification, not the assessment instance.

Guided practice. For a=(1,0), b=(0,1), c=(1,1), remove c because c=a+b; the target (2,3) has (a,b)-coordinates (2,3). Its dot with (1,0) is 2 and the cosine is 2/sqrt(13), not 2.

Distinction check. Another valid basis may yield different coefficients for the same target. Score the basis proof and consistency of coordinates, not just one favored pair. A zero comparison direction would make the angle undefined.

Choose any two that form a basis for the span of the library and justify both redundancy of the omitted vector and independence of your chosen pair. Determine whether t=(3,-1,1) is in that span and give its coordinates relative to your stated ordered basis. Finally, for d=(1,0,-1), compute t·d and the cosine of the angle between t and d, checking the nonzero conditions.
rubricEvidence: Computes t·d=2 and both positive norms sqrt(11),sqrt(2).
Computes cos θ=2/sqrt(22) with nonzero-denominator justification.
T22V3::ARC511::S17@1.why: The learner computes dot, norms and normalized cosine with nonzero check.

T22V3::ARC511::S17@1.claim: Diagnose combined false claims about dependence, membership and an angle to zero.
publicRequestExact: Audit this report about p=(1,0,2), q=(0,2,1), r=(1,2,3), and target s=(2,2,3) in R³: “The three generators are independent because no pair is parallel; s is reachable because there are three of them; and the angle between s and zero is π/2 since their dot product is zero.” For each assertion give a mathematical correction or counterexample, with a zero relation, an all-combination obstruction, and the relevant angle condition.
rubricEvidence: Refutes independence with the nontrivial relation p+q-r=0.
Derives an invariant for all combinations and uses it to prove s is unreachable.
Rejects the zero-vector angle claim using the nonzero/denominator condition.
T22V3::ARC511::S17@1.why: The learner repairs dependence, span and zero-angle errors separately.
T22V3::ARC511::S17@1.escapeAttempt: Correcting only one of the three false claims does not satisfy the synthesis.
